Repo locks

A lock on a repository's refs - its main branch, or a tag pattern - that agents on several machines declare once and hold while they land changes, so landings happen one at a time.

On this page
  • A lock belongs to a repository
  • Declared once, keyed by the origin
  • Holding a lock

A repo lock guards a repository's refs - its main branch, or a pattern such as every release tag - so that agents working on several machines land their changes one at a time. An agent declares a repository's lock once, takes it before it lands, and lets it go when the refs have landed. While one agent holds the lock, another agent's attempt to take it is refused, naming the holder (when the asker may see that session), since when it has held it and until when.

Repo locks are an optional feature, off by default. Turn them on in the console under Settings → Features (Repo locks), or in the configuration file with features.repo_locks: true, or with SEAMLESS_FEATURES_REPO_LOCKS=true. While the feature is off, the four locks_* tools are neither listed nor callable, the Locks screen is gone, and seam lock says the feature is off. Turning it off deletes no lock.

A lock belongs to a repository

A lock is never a project's. Project mappings are path prefixes, not repositories: one mapping can cover many repositories, a repository can be carved out of it for another project, and sessions of two projects work in one repository by design. A lock owned by a project could not be unique, and two projects could each lock the same repository and split the mutex. So a lock has no project, and every surface shows it with its repository and its name: LOCK seamless main.

A lock carries no free text either. Its state is the resource (its guarded refs), the holder (a session), since and until.

Declared once, keyed by the origin

seam lock declare (or the locks_declare tool) declares a lock from inside the repository's checkout. The repository is named by its git identity, which seam lock reads on its own machine:

  • The origin URL is the key. It is normalized, so the ssh and https forms of one repository (git@host:owner/repo.git, https://host/owner/repo) are one lock, from every machine.
  • Host and path are the fallback. A repository with no origin is locked by its machine and its main checkout root. Every checkout seen is recorded the same way, so a repository that gains or changes its origin keeps its lock.
  • A side clone is its origin's repository. A clone whose origin is a local path is a checkout of the repository at that path.

A second declaration of the same repository and name, from any project or any machine, returns the first lock unchanged and only records the new checkout's identity on it. Two locks on one repository and name cannot exist.

A lock's name is a token (main by default, or release), and it guards refs/heads/<name> unless the declaration names other refs: full ref names under refs/, or patterns with one *, such as refs/tags/v*. A declaration also lists the projects whose restricted accounts may hold the lock (by default the project the checkout maps to).

A declaration from a restricted account waits for the owner: it is stored as requested, nobody can hold it, and the owner approves or discards it on the console's Locks page. Everyone else declares directly.

Holding a lock

Holding a lock works the way claiming a task does, with the same compare-and-set:

  • Acquire takes a free lock for the current session, with a lease (900 seconds by default, at most 4 hours).
  • Heartbeat is acquiring again: the holder's lease is refreshed, and the hold keeps the time it began.
  • A lapsed lease is free. A hold is live only while its lease has not run out; at the moment it expires, another session may take the lock, and the answer says it took over a lapsed hold.
  • Release lets the lock go; only the holder may.
  • Force-release is the owner's override, on the console's Locks page (or seam lock release --force): it ends any hold, live or lapsed.
  • A hold keeps its session live. While its lease is live, the idle reaper does not end the session holding it, however quiet its landing goes, as with a live task claim.
  • A session's holds end with it. session_end and the SessionEnd hook free every lock the session holds; the reaper frees the lapsed holds of a session it ends.
  • A lost hold is news to its holder. A holder whose lapsed hold another session took, whose hold the owner force-released, or whose lapsed hold the reaper freed is told once, as for a lost claim: a Lock lost: ... line naming the lock by id and name.

A lock is a coordination signal between cooperating agents: holding one tells every other agent that the refs it guards are being landed. It does not, by itself, stop anyone from pushing.
